title: I am the vine (John 15:1–8)
hookLine: abide in me; the branch can't bear fruit alone

lines: A CUT BRANCH LOOKS FINE FOR A DAY.
THE VINE: AN OLD PICTURE FOR ISRAEL.
cards: Cut a branch off a grapevine and lay it on the kitchen counter. For a day it looks fine: green leaves, maybe a few small grapes. You could put it in a vase and fool a guest.
By the end of the week it's curling and brown. Nothing went wrong with the branch itself. It just isn't attached to anything anymore.
And the vine was an old picture for Israel itself in the Psalms and the prophets. So on his last night, Jesus reaches for an image the people at the table knew well.

teach.h: I AM THE TRUE VINE; MY FATHER, THE FARMER.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman." Husbandman is an old word for farmer, here the vinedresser who prunes.
Then the center of the passage: "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me." Abide.

teach.h: MENO: TO STAY, TO REMAIN, TO LIVE THERE.
teach.b: The Greek verb is meno: to stay, to remain, to live somewhere and not leave. In the first chapter, two disciples asked Jesus where he was staying, and they came and stayed with him that day. Same verb.
Here, in a few short verses, it keeps coming back, like a refrain. Notice what Jesus does not say. He doesn't say try harder to produce fruit.

teach.h: BRANCHES DON'T STRAIN; THEY STAY ATTACHED.
teach.b: Branches don't strain. Fruit is simply what happens when the sap gets through. The work is staying attached.

teach.h: THE FARMER PRUNES FOR A HARVEST.
teach.b: There's a harder edge, too: the farmer prunes.

teach.h: I AM THE VINE, YE ARE THE BRANCHES.
teach.b: Branches that bear fruit are cut back so they'll bear more, and branches cut off from the vine wither and are gathered and burned.

Christians read that pruning in different ways: as discipline, as loss that leads to growth, or as the warning it sounds like. Some readers find comfort in it too: a vinedresser cuts because he expects a harvest.
Then the line that sums it up: "I am the vine, ye are the branches." Not I am the trunk and you hang off me somewhere. One plant.

how: Christians speak of abiding in Christ through prayer, scripture, worship and, in many churches, Communion.

o: to wait patiently for something to arrive
to stay, remain, and make your home somewhere
to obey a rule even when you don't like it

games.q: what's inside John 15:1–8 — tap the pairs.
p: the farmer who prunes the vine
looks fine for a day, then withers
what comes when the branch stays on

s: the vine was a new image Jesus invented
the vine was already an old picture for Israel in the Psalms and the prophets.
in the passage, the Father is the husbandman who tends the vine
"I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman."
in the passage, branches bear fruit by trying harder
fruit comes from staying attached: "except it abide in the vine."

games.q: you're a branch on a vine, and you want to bear fruit. what does the passage say you do?
o: move to a better spot in the vineyard.
games.why: abide: "as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me."

practice: Ask yourself what actually feeds you, not what distracts you or fills the time, but what sends life through you: a friendship, prayer, music, scripture, a long walk, a table with people you love.

Notice how long it's been since you were really connected to it, without scolding yourself, and stay with it for these minutes, the way a branch stays on a vine. If you pray, simply rest in the words abide in me.

wordCard.voice: Abide. In Greek, meno: to stay, to remain, to make your home somewhere. The branch's whole job, in John's picture, is to stay attached.

orig.note: Greek: I stay, I remain, I dwell. John comes back to this verb again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: find what feeds you. Branches don't strain; they stay. That's day six hundred thirty-four.
